claim: Slc6a14 is expressed predominantly in the wild-type mouse colon (C57BL/6N).
source: Quantification of relative mRNA expression by qRT-PCR revealed that Slc6a14 is expressed predominantly in the wild-type mouse colon (C57BL/6N Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a demonstrating highest expression in colon compared to other tissues.

claim: SLC6A14 was localized at the apical pole on the apical surface in mouse colonic organoids.
source: We found that SLC6A14 was localized at the apical pole on the apical surface, as expected (Figure 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy of colonic organoids transduced with SLC6A14-GFP showing apical localization.

claim: The Slc6a14(-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport compared to wild-type mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that the Slc6a14 (-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport (Figure 1e), suggesting that Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
evidence: Measured using ex vivo closed loop assay with 3H-arginine uptake, shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
source: Interestingly, we found that the Slc6a14 (-/y) mice exhibited ~ 75% reduction in apical arginine transport (Figure 1e), suggesting that Slc6a14 constitutes a major apical arginine uptake pathway in the mouse colon.
evidence: Inferred from the 75% reduction in arginine transport when Slc6a14 is knocked out.

claim: The steady state levels of arginine were lower in the Slc6a14 knock-out colonic epithelium compared to wild-type epithelium.
source: We performed mass spectrometry using freshly lysed tissue, and found that the steady state levels of arginine were indeed lower in the Slc6a14 knock-out colonic epithelium (steady state L-arginine = L-arginine/(L-citrulline + L-ornithine)), compared to wild-type epithelium (Figure 1f).
evidence: Measured by mass spectrometry of freshly lysed tissue, shown in Figure 1f as arginine bioavailability.

claim: Decrease in amino acid uptake across the colonic epithelium did not affect serum amino acid levels.
source: Interestingly, decrease in amino acid uptake across the colonic epithelium did not affect serum amino acid levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by serum amino acid analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The F508del mutation in mice results in an intestinal phenotype of varying severity, which is dependent on the genetic background of the mouse.
source: It is known that the F508del mutation in mice results in an intestinal phenotype of varying severity, which is dependent on the genetic background of the mouse (Rozmahel et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rozmahel et al., 1996.

claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 in CF mice (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(-/y)) led to a further reduction in weight gain and BMI post weaning (day 34), relative to age matched controls.
source: As shown in Figure 2, disruption of Slc6a14 in CF mice (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(-/y)) led to a further reduction in weight gain and BMI post weaning (day 34), relative to age matched controls, (Cftr(F508del/F508del) Slc6a14(+/y)) (Figure 2a,b,c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by weight and BMI measurements shown in Figure 2a, b, c.

claim: The defect in weight gain in double mutant mice was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age.
source: While this defect in weight gain was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age, it was associated with increased mortality during this period (Figure 2d).
evidence: Shown by weight tracking data and survival curves in Figure 2d.

claim: The defect in weight gain in double mutant mice was associated with increased mortality during the post-weaning period.
source: While this defect in weight gain was temporary in nature, with the double mutant mice recovering to the same weight as the F508del mice by 56 days in age, it was associated with increased mortality during this period (Figure 2d).
evidence: Demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival curves in Figure 2d showing significantly lower survival in double mutant mice.

claim: CF mice exhibit reduced weights relative to their wild-type siblings early in life after weaning.
source: It has been previously reported that CF mice exhibit reduced weights relative to their wild-type siblings early in life after weaning (van Doorninck et al., 1995), and we confirmed this defect in the current experiment at day 34 after birth, in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) mice (Figure 2).
evidence: Confirmed by weight measurements at day 34 shown in Figure 2, and supported by citation to van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claim: The CF-related smooth muscle thickening phenotype in the distal ileum and colon was worse when Slc6a14 was disrupted.
source: Interestingly, we also found that the CF-related smooth muscle thickening phenotype in the distal ileum and colon was worse when Slc6a14 was disrupted (Figure 3a,b,c and d).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 3a-d showing increased smooth muscle area in double mutant mice.

claim: cAMP induced CFTR-mediated fluid accumulation was decreased in intestinal segments derived from mice, homozygous for F508del-Cftr.
source: As previously reported, cyclic AMP (cAMP) induced CFTR-mediated fluid accumulation was decreased in intestinal segments derived from mice, homozygous for F508del-Cftr (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Measured by in-situ closed loop assay shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 in the CF mice further worsened the secretory defect.
source: Importantly, disruption of Slc6a14 in the CF mice, further worsened this secretory defect (Figure 4b).
evidence: Demonstrated by in-situ closed loop assay showing lower fluid secretion in double mutant mice compared to F508del mice, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Slc6a14 disruption alone impaired cAMP-induced secretion relative to that in wild-type (C57BL/6N background) siblings.
source: Interestingly, Slc6a14 disruption alone impaired cAMP-induced secretion relative to that in wild-type (C57BL/6N background) siblings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by closed loop assay in C57BL/6N background mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in fluid secretion in Slc6a14 knockout mice was not due to change in Cftr mRNA expression.
source: This decrease in fluid secretion was not due to change in Cftr mRNA expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and the basis for this change is investigated in subsequent studies.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR showing no significant difference in Cftr mRNA levels, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FIS response was significantly lower in the colonic organoids from double mutant mice (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)), compared to the F508del-CF mice.
source: As expected from the above 'closed loop' studies, the FIS response was significantly lower in the colonic organoids from double mutant mice (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)), compared to the F508del-CF mice (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Measured by forskolin-induced swelling assay in colonic organoids, shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: SLC6A14 is a major apical arginine transporter in the colonic epithelium of wild-type and F508del mice, on the FVB background.
source: We confirmed that SLC6A14 is a major apical arginine transporter in the colonic epithelium of wild-type and F508del mice, on the FVB background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by ex vivo closed loop arginine uptake assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute pre-addition of L-arginine (1 mM) on the apical surface increased the residual, cAMP-activated function of F508del-CFTR in split-open organoids derived from F508del-mice at 27°C.
source: Importantly, we found that acute pre-addition of L-arginine (1 mM) on the apical surface, increased the residual, cAMP-activated function of F508del-CFTR in split-open organoids derived from F508del-mice at 27°C (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Measured by ACC assay in split-open organoids at 27°C, shown in Figure 5c and d (note: text references Figure 6a and b but should be Figure 5c and d based on figure numbering).

claim: The arginine-dependent enhancement effect on F508del-CFTR function was lacking in tissues obtained from the double mutant mice, lacking SLC6A14.
source: This arginine-dependent enhancement effect was lacking in tissues obtained from the double mutant mice, lacking SLC6A14 (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay showing no enhancement with arginine in double mutant organoids, shown in Figure 5d.

claim: F508del-CFTR channel function upon FSK stimulation was still detectable at 37°C, albeit reduced in comparison to measurements acquired at 27°C.
source: F508del-CFTR channel function upon FSK stimulation was still detectable at this temperature, albeit reduced in comparison to measurements acquired at 27°C (Figure 5e,f), reflecting the sensitivity of the ACC assay.
evidence: Measured by ACC assay at 37°C shown in Figure 5e and f.

claim: Residual mutant F508del-CFTR function at 37°C was enhanced by pre-addition of L-arginine on the apical surface in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) murine organoids, but not from those derived from the tissue of double mutant (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)) mice.
source: Further, as in the preceding experiments, this residual mutant CFTR function, was enhanced by pre-addition of L-arginine on the apical surface in the Cftr(F508del/F508del) murine organoids, but not from those derived from the tissue of double mutant (CftrF508del/F508del; Slc6a14(-/y)) mice (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay at 37°C shown in Figure 5e and f.

claim: The cAMP-stimulated CFTR function was lower in the double mutant-derived organoids compared to F508del organoids.
source: Also, the cAMP-stimulated CFTR function was lower in the double mutant-derived organoids.
evidence: Inferred from ACC assay data comparing F508del and double mutant organoids.

claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein.
source: We found that over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), nor did it alter the cell surface stability of the rescued protein.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 did not alter the cell surface stability of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein.
source: We found that over-expression of SLC6A14 did not affect the processing of the temperature rescued F508del-CFTR protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), nor did it alter the cell surface stability of the rescued protein.
evidence: Demonstrated by cycloheximide chase assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no significant effect of SLC6A14 expression on the processing or stability of human F508del-CFTR.
source: Therefore, there was no significant effect of SLC6A14 expression on the processing or stability of human F508del-CFTR.
evidence: Concluded from western blot and cycloheximide chase experiments in BHK cells.

claim: Reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of SLC6A14 and F508del-CFTR was not detected.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4, we did not detect reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of the two membrane proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Induced NOS (iNOS) is expressed in mouse colonic tissue.
source: As shown in Figure 6a, the SLC6A14 substrate, arginine, is converted to nitric oxide (NO) by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), and we found that induced NOS (iNOS) is expressed in mouse colonic tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by PCR showing iNOS mRNA expression in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nitric oxide activates F508del-CFTR channel function.
source: In the current work, we showed nitric oxide (NO) also activates F508del-CFTR channel function.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments with NO donor GSNO enhancing forskolin response.

claim: The forskolin response measured in split-open organoids from CftrF508del/F508del mice was enhanced by the NO donor GSNO.
source: Specifically, the forskolin response measured in split-open organoids from CftrF508del/F508del mice was enhanced by the NO donor GSNO (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay with GSNO treatment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The positive effect of arginine on forskolin activated F508del channel function was reduced by pretreatment with the iNOS inhibitor 1400W in organoids derived from CftrF508del/F508del mice.
source: We found that the positive effect of arginine on forskolin activated F508del channel function was reduced by pretreatment with the iNOS inhibitor 1400W in organoids derived from CftrF508del/F508del mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay with 1400W pretreatment shown in Figure 6b and c.

claim: The 1400W sensitive effect of arginine on F508del-CFTR was dependent on SLC6A14 expression.
source: Further the 1400W sensitive effect of arginine was dependent on SLC6A14 expression (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing effects in F508del vs double mutant organoids in Figure 6b and c.

claim: Colonic epithelial tissue derived from Slc6a14 knock-out mice exhibited lower constitutive NO levels.
source: As shown in Figure 6d, colonic epithelial tissue derived from Slc6a14 knock-out mice exhibited lower constitutive NO levels.
evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6d.

claim: There was an increase in NO production evoked by acute addition of arginine (1 mM) to the apical surface of split-open colonic organoids obtained from wild-type mice, but this increase was abrogated in split-open organoids generated from Slc6a14(-/y) littermates.
source: Interestingly, while there was an increase in NO production evoked by acute addition of arginine (1 mM) to the apical surface of split-open colonic organoids obtained from wild-type mice, this increase was abrogated in split-open organoids generated from Slc6a14(-/y) littermates (Figure 6e–f).
evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence assay shown in Figure 6e and f.

claim: Slc6a14-mediated arginine uptake is important for NO synthesis.
source: Altogether, these data show that Slc6a14-mediated arginine uptake is important for NO synthesis, and hence NO mediated signaling to the CFTR channel.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing reduced NO levels and arginine-stimulated NO production in Slc6a14 knockout mice.

claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO.
source: Conversely, over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO and enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids (Figure 6g–i).
evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence in SLC6A14-GFP transduced organoids shown in Figure 6g-i.

claim: Over-expression of SLC6A14 enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids.
source: Conversely, over-expression of SLC6A14 via lentivirus transduction conferred increased constitutive levels of NO and enhanced the increase in cytosolic NO after addition of arginine to the apical surface of split-open organoids (Figure 6g–i).
evidence: Measured by DAF-FM fluorescence in SLC6A14-GFP transduced organoids shown in Figure 6g-i.

claim: PKA-mediated activation of Wt-CFTR function can be enhanced by the NO donors GSNO and SNP, and by the downstream signaling molecule cGMP.
source: Using the ACC assay (Ahmadi et al., 2017), to measure CFTR channel function, we found that PKA-mediated activation of Wt-CFTR function can be enhanced by the NO donors GSNO and SNP, and by the downstream signaling molecule cGMP.
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay in Caco-2 cells shown in Figure 7b and c.

claim: The effect of GSNO on PKA-activated CFTR channel function is abolished in presence of protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823.
source: This effect of GSNO on PKA-activated CFTR channel function is abolished in presence of protein kinase G (PKG) inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823 (Figure 7b,c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay in Caco-2 cells with PKG inhibitors shown in Figure 7b, c, and d.

claim: PKA-dependent channel activity of CFTR is enhanced by NO-mediated activation of PKG in Caco-2 colonic epithelial cell line.
source: Thus, we show that PKA-dependent channel activity of CFTR is enhanced by NO-mediated activation of PKG, in this colonic epithelial cell line, highlighting the importance of this signaling pathway for CFTR function in a model of human colon.
evidence: Concluded from experiments with NO donors and PKG inhibitors in Caco-2 cells.

claim: CFTR function was enhanced by pre-activation of SLC6A14 with arginine, only in the Caco-2 cell line over-expressing SLC6A14.
source: Using the CFTR functional assay described above, we found that CFTR function (measured as CFTRinh-172 response) was enhanced by pre-activation of SLC6A14 with arginine, only in the Caco-2 cell line over-expressing SLC6A14.
evidence: Demonstrated by FLIPR membrane potential assay in Caco-2 cells shown in Figure 7e and f.

claim: Enhancement of CFTR function by SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport could be inhibited by PKG specific inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823, as well as the iNOS inhibitor 1440W.
source: This enhancement of CFTR function by SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport could be inhibited by PKG specific inhibitors Rp-8-pCPT-cGMPS and KT5823, as well as the iNOS inhibitor 1440W (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: Demonstrated by FLIPR membrane potential assay in Caco-2 cells with inhibitors shown in Figure 7e and f.

claim: SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport can enhance CFTR function via the NO signaling pathway, in Caco-2 cells.
source: Taken together, we show that SLC6A14-mediated arginine transport can enhance CFTR function via the NO signaling pathway, in Caco-2 cells.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing arginine enhancement of CFTR function that is blocked by iNOS and PKG inhibitors.

claim: Pre-treatment of split-open organoids from double mutant mice with membrane permeable cGMP (8Br-cGMP) enhanced forskolin-activated F508del-CFTR channel activity partially towards that observed in tissues from F508del mice with native SLC6A14 expression at 27°C.
source: Interestingly, we found that pre-treatment of split-open organoids from double mutant mice, with membrane permeable cGMP (8Br-cGMP), enhanced forskolin-activated F508del-CFTR channel activity partially towards that observed in tissues from F508del mice with native SLC6A14 expression (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay at 27°C shown in Figure 8a and b.

claim: The partial rescue effect induced by 8Br-cGMP pre-treatment was recapitulated at physiological temperature (37°C) in the organoid swelling assay.
source: Importantly, the partial rescue effect induced by 8Br-cGMP pre-treatment was recapitulated at physiological temperature in the organoid swelling assay (Figure 8c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by forskolin-induced swelling assay at 37°C shown in Figure 8c and d.

claim: Pre-treatment of organoids from double mutant mice with cGMP restored forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) to approximately 50% of the swelling measured in F508del-CFTR organoids, at 37°C.
source: Specifically, pre-treatment of organoids from double mutant mice with cGMP restored forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) to approximately 50% of the swelling measured in F508del-CFTR organoids, at 37°C.
evidence: Quantified from organoid swelling assay data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The arginine transport activity of SLC6A14 and the downstream signaling via NO regulated cGMP plays an important role in modifying F508del-CFTR channel function and F508del-CFTR-mediated secretion.
source: Together, these findings support the hypothesis that the arginine transport activity of SLC6A14 and the downstream signaling via NO regulated cGMP plays an important role in modifying F508del-CFTR channel function and F508del-CFTR-mediated secretion.
evidence: Concluded from experiments showing cGMP rescue of F508del-CFTR function in double mutant organoids.

claim: SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del.
source: This work provides a mechanism whereby SLC6A14, previously identified as a genetic modifier of CF disease severity, can ameliorate the primary CF-causing defect. We found that SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium and in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del, and its arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion.
evidence: Demonstrated by arginine uptake assays and functional studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: SLC6A14's arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion in CF mice.
source: This work provides a mechanism whereby SLC6A14, previously identified as a genetic modifier of CF disease severity, can ameliorate the primary CF-causing defect. We found that SLC6A14 is a major arginine transporter on the apical surface of the colonic epithelium and in mice modeling the major CF-causing mutation F508del, and its arginine transport function can ameliorate the basic defect in fluid secretion.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluid secretion assays and organoid swelling studies showing worsened defects when SLC6A14 is absent.

claim: SLC6A14 has been identified as a genetic modifier of multiple CF disease outcomes, including meconium ileus, lung disease, and the age of first infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: SLC6A14 has been identified as a genetic modifier of multiple CF disease outcomes, including meconium ileus (Sun et al., 2012), lung disease (Corvol et al., 2015) and the age of first infection by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2012; Corvol et al., 2015; and Li et al., 2014.

claim: The pleiotropic effect of SLC6A14 supports the hypothesis that it modifies the basic defect responsible for disease in multiple organs, namely the defect in anion conduction.
source: This pleiotropic effect supports the hypothesis that it modifies the basic defect responsible for disease in multiple organs, namely the defect in anion conduction.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SLC6A14 affects multiple CF disease outcomes.

claim: The intestinal phenotypes associated with the primary CF defect in mice, namely defective secretory capacity with thickened smooth muscle, were worsened by disruption of Slc6a14 expression.
source: In support of the above hypothesis, we found that the intestinal phenotypes associated with the primary CF defect in mice, namely defective secretory capacity with thickened smooth muscle, were worsened by disruption of Slc6a14 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluid secretion assays and histological analysis showing worsened phenotypes in double mutant mice.

claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 expression in mice bearing Wt-CFTR did not cause profound changes in colonic morphology, function or mouse survival.
source: Interestingly, disruption of Slc6a14 expression in mice bearing Wt-CFTR did not cause profound changes in colonic morphology (IMPC, 2018), function or mouse survival.
evidence: Supported by reference to IMPC, 2018 and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claim: Disruption of Slc6a14 did impair arginine uptake across the apical membrane of colonic epithelium in Wt-Cftr C57Bl/6 mice.
source: However, disruption of Slc6a14 did impair arginine uptake across the apical membrane of colonic epithelium in Wt-Cftr C57Bl/6 mice (Figure 1e), and impaired cAMP-mediated fluid secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by arginine uptake assay in Figure 1e and fluid secretion assay in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: This arginine transporter on the apical membrane of colonic epithelium has a dominant role in CFTR regulation rather than nutrient uptake.
source: Together, these observations support the hypothesis that this arginine transporter on the apical membrane of colonic epithelium has a dominant role in CFTR regulation rather than nutrient uptake, as amino acid uptake normally occurs in the small intestine.
evidence: Inferred from observations that Slc6a14 knockout affects CFTR function but not serum amino acid levels, and that amino acid uptake normally occurs in the small intestine.

claim: The negative consequences of the F508del mutation on folding and assembly of the mouse CFTR protein are somewhat less severe than in human CFTR protein, hence there is residual epithelial expression and function being detected in this organism.
source: In contrast to the consequences of the F508del mutation in the human CFTR protein, the negative consequences of this mutation in folding and assembly of the mouse CFTR protein are somewhat less severe, hence there is residual epithelial expression and function being detected in this organism (Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995; Wilke et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995; and Wilke et al., 2011.

claim: A significant amount of the mutant mouse F508del-CFTR protein will reach the surface and function.
source: As previously published, this reflects a less deleterious effect of the mutation on the folding, assembly and maturation, such that a significant amount of the mutant mouse protein (still less that wild-type) will reach the surface and function (French et al., 1996; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to French et al., 1996; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Scholte et al., 2004; and van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claim: The extent of modulation by SLC6A14 in the colonic epithelium of CF patients with the F508del mutation will depend on its residual expression levels at the apical membrane of this epithelium, or the abundance of this mutant at the cell surface after correction with Lumacaftor.
source: We predict that the extent of modulation by SLC6A14 in the colonic epithelium of CF patients with the F508del mutation will depend on its residual expression levels at the apical membrane of this epithelium, or the abundance of this mutant at the cell surface after correction with Lumacaftor.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings that SLC6A14 modulates F508del-CFTR function.

claim: The modulation of F508del-CFTR by SLC6A14 is dependent, at least in part, on arginine-mediated NO production and PKG activation.
source: Our findings suggest that the modulation of F508del-CFTR by SLC6A14 is dependent, at least in part, on arginine-mediated NO production and PKG activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing that iNOS and PKG inhibitors block the effect of arginine on F508del-CFTR function.

claim: The role of the arginine-NO pathway has been well studied in models of CF.
source: The role of the arginine-NO pathway has been well studied in models of CF (Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann et al., 1997; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; Grasemann et al., 2005; Oliynyk et al., 2013; Poschet et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies of the arginine-NO pathway in CF.

claim: The downstream regulators of the arginine-NO pathway, cGMP and PKG, can enhance wild-type and mutant CFTR channel function and trafficking.
source: At the molecular level, it is known that the downstream regulators of this pathway, cGMP and PKG, can enhance wild-type and mutant CFTR channel function and trafficking (Golin-Bisello et al., 2005; Leier et al., 2012; Poschet et al., 2007; Vaandrager et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Golin-Bisello et al., 2005; Leier et al., 2012; Poschet et al., 2007; and Vaandrager et al., 1997.

claim: Previous studies of mouse derived intestinal organoids showed that agonists of PKG are effective in enhancing CFTR-mediated organoid swelling, in the absence of agonists of the canonical regulation of CFTR, such as PKA.
source: Previous studies of mouse derived intestinal organoids showed that agonists of PKG are effective in enhancing CFTR-mediated organoid swelling, in the absence of agonists of the canonical regulation of CFTR, such as PKA (Pattison et al., 2016; Picciotto et al., 1992; Seidler et al., 1997; Vaandrager et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pattison et al., 2016; Picciotto et al., 1992; Seidler et al., 1997; and Vaandrager et al., 1997.

claim: PKG-mediated phosphorylation exerts a 'priming' effect on the canonical PKA-mediated activation of CFTR.
source: Our studies confirm the functional significance of this regulatory pathway in murine colon, and further, our findings suggest that PKG-mediated phosphorylation exerts a 'priming' effect on the canonical PKA-mediated activation of CFTR.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that NO/cGMP enhances PKA-mediated CFTR activation.

claim: There are five sites at which CFTR can be phosphorylated by PKG.
source: There are five sites at which CFTR can be phosphorylated by PKG (NetPhosK v3, consensus strength >0.5).
evidence: Predicted by NetPhosK v3 bioinformatics tool.

claim: Two PKG phosphorylation sites are localized in the regulatory 'R' domain of CFTR, at position 788 and 795, which overlap with the consensus site for PKA phosphorylation.
source: Two are localized in the regulatory 'R' domain, at position 788 and 795, which overlap with the consensus site for PKA phosphorylation (Pasyk et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pasyk et al., 2015 and bioinformatics prediction.

claim: The strength of the consensus sites for PKG at position 788 is predicted to exceed that of PKA, and may be preferentially phosphorylated by PKG.
source: Interestingly, the strength of the consensus sites for PKG at position 788 is predicted to exceed that of PKA, and may be preferentially phosphorylated by PKG.
evidence: Predicted by bioinformatics analysis of phosphorylation consensus sites.

claim: cGMP partially rescued the defects in cAMP-induced channel activation and organoid swelling in colonic tissue lacking SLC6A14.
source: Both of our assays of regulated F508del-CFTR channel function in colonic tissue lacking SLC6A14 showed that cGMP partially rescued the defects in cAMP-induced channel activation and organoid swelling.
evidence: Demonstrated by ACC assay and organoid swelling assay with 8Br-cGMP treatment shown in Figure 8.

claim: The augmentation by cGMP did not fully restore F508del-CFTR functions to those observed in tissues obtained from F508del mice expressing native Slc6a14.
source: However, while significant, this augmentation did not fully restore these functions to those observed in tissues obtained from F508del mice (expressing native Slc6a14).
evidence: Observed from quantitative comparison of cGMP rescue effects in Figure 8.

claim: There could be other, yet unidentified, signaling pathways involved in SLC6A14-mediated CFTR modulation.
source: Hence, there could be other, yet unidentified, signaling pathways involved in SLC6A14-mediated CFTR modulation.
evidence: Speculated based on the incomplete rescue by cGMP.

claim: The doubly mutated mice may harbor secondary, chronic consequences, which impact F508del-Cftr.
source: Alternatively, the doubly mutated mice may harbor secondary, chronic consequences, which impact F508del-Cftr, and we will assess such consequences in future studies.
evidence: Speculated as an alternative explanation for incomplete rescue by cGMP.

claim: Upregulation of Slc6a14 expression and SLC6A14-mediated arginine uptake will ameliorate the disease phenotype associated with Cftr mutation.
source: The current findings suggest that upregulation of Slc6a14 expression and SLC6A14-mediated arginine uptake will ameliorate the disease phenotype associated with Cftr mutation.
evidence: Inferred from findings that SLC6A14 enhances F508del-CFTR function and that its loss worsens CF phenotype.

claim: Patients with CF have a decreased concentration of exhaled NO.
source: Interestingly, studies by Grasemann and colleagues showed that patients with CF have a decreased concentration of exhaled NO (Grasemann et al., 1997), related to decreased nitric-oxide synthase (iNOS) activity, increased cellular arginase activity, and decreased arginine bioavailability (Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; Grasemann et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grasemann et al., 1997; Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; and Grasemann et al., 2005.

claim: Decreased exhaled NO in CF patients is related to decreased nitric-oxide synthase (iNOS) activity, increased cellular arginase activity, and decreased arginine bioavailability.
source: Interestingly, studies by Grasemann and colleagues showed that patients with CF have a decreased concentration of exhaled NO (Grasemann et al., 1997), related to decreased nitric-oxide synthase (iNOS) activity, increased cellular arginase activity, and decreased arginine bioavailability (Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; Grasemann et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grasemann et al., 2011; Grasemann and Ratjen, 2012; and Grasemann et al., 2005.

claim: The mechanism underlying decreased arginine bioavailability in CF is unknown.
source: The mechanism underlying decreased arginine bioavailability in CF is unknown, but we propose that this deficit worsens the channel function of the low, residual levels of F508del-CFTR and that increased SLC6A14 expression will offset this deficit.
evidence: Stated as unknown in the literature.

claim: Decreased arginine bioavailability in CF worsens the channel function of the low, residual levels of F508del-CFTR.
source: The mechanism underlying decreased arginine bioavailability in CF is unknown, but we propose that this deficit worsens the channel function of the low, residual levels of F508del-CFTR and that increased SLC6A14 expression will offset this deficit.
evidence: Proposed based on findings that arginine enhances F508del-CFTR function via SLC6A14.

claim: Increased SLC6A14 expression will offset the deficit in arginine bioavailability in CF.
source: The mechanism underlying decreased arginine bioavailability in CF is unknown, but we propose that this deficit worsens the channel function of the low, residual levels of F508del-CFTR and that increased SLC6A14 expression will offset this deficit.
evidence: Proposed based on findings that SLC6A14 overexpression increases NO levels and enhances CFTR function.

claim: An increase in SLC6A14-mediated arginine uptake would be expected to overcome decreased arginine bioavailability in CF tissues, and enhance NO and cGMP-mediated 'priming' of F508del-CFTR channel activity at the cell surface.
source: An increase in SLC6A14-mediated arginine uptake would be expected to overcome decreased arginine bioavailability in CF tissues, and enhance NO and cGMP-mediated 'priming' of F508del-CFTR channel activity at the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing SLC6A14 enhances arginine uptake, NO production, and F508del-CFTR function.

claim: Bacterial products enhance the expression of SLC6A14 in primary cultures of airway epithelium derived from CF patients.
source: Although not specifically tested in this study, we showed in primary cultures of airway epithelium derived from CF patients that bacterial products enhance the expression of SLC6A14 (Di Paola et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Paola et al., 2017.

claim: The bacterial load in the colon of patients will be high.
source: As the bacterial load in the colon of patients will be high (Pereira and Berry, 2017), we expect that SLC6A14 expression will be upregulated and poised to modify any mutant CFTR protein that exhibits residual channel function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pereira and Berry, 2017.

claim: SLC6A14 expression will be upregulated in the colon and poised to modify any mutant CFTR protein that exhibits residual channel function.
source: As the bacterial load in the colon of patients will be high (Pereira and Berry, 2017), we expect that SLC6A14 expression will be upregulated and poised to modify any mutant CFTR protein that exhibits residual channel function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that bacterial products upregulate SLC6A14 and the colon has high bacterial load.

claim: It has yet to be determined if the modification by SLC6A14 is dependent on the genotype of GWAS-identified SNPs.
source: Finally, it has yet to be determined if this modification by SLC6A14 is dependent on the genotype of GWAS-identified SNPs.
evidence: Stated as an open question for future research.

claim: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disorder, caused by mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene.
source: Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disorder, caused by mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene (Kartner et al., 1991; Li et al., 1993; Riordan et al., 1989; Rommens et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kartner et al., 1991; Li et al., 1993; Riordan et al., 1989; and Rommens et al., 1989.

claim: The CFTR protein is primarily expressed in epithelial cells lining the airways, intestinal tract, and tubular organs.
source: The CFTR protein is primarily expressed in epithelial cells lining the airways, intestinal tract, and tubular organs, where its anion channel activity on the apical membrane drives fluid transport and modulates the pH of elaborated fluid (Bear et al., 1992; Li et al., 1993; Quinton, 1990; Shah et al., 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bear et al., 1992; Li et al., 1993; Quinton, 1990; and Shah et al., 2016a, 2016b.

claim: CFTR's anion channel activity on the apical membrane drives fluid transport and modulates the pH of elaborated fluid.
source: The CFTR protein is primarily expressed in epithelial cells lining the airways, intestinal tract, and tubular organs, where its anion channel activity on the apical membrane drives fluid transport and modulates the pH of elaborated fluid (Bear et al., 1992; Li et al., 1993; Quinton, 1990; Shah et al., 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bear et al., 1992; Li et al., 1993; Quinton, 1990; and Shah et al., 2016a, 2016b.

claim: It is the loss of CFTR channel function, caused by CFTR mutations, that triggers pathogenesis in CF.
source: It is the loss of this channel function, caused by CFTR mutations, that triggers pathogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the CF field.

claim: The severity of CF disease amongst individuals harboring the same genetic mutation is variable.
source: However, the severity of disease amongst individuals harboring the same genetic mutation is variable (Kerem et al., 1990; Kerem and Kerem, 1996; Luisetti, 1997; Rosenstein, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerem et al., 1990; Kerem and Kerem, 1996; Luisetti, 1997; and Rosenstein, 1994.

claim: Decrease in lung function over time is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality in CF patients.
source: Decrease in lung function over time is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality in CF patients (Gilljam et al., 2004; Kerem and Kerem, 1996) and recent genome-wide association studies have identified polymorphisms in several secondary genetic factors associate with CF lung disease severity (Corvol et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilljam et al., 2004 and Kerem and Kerem, 1996.

claim: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified polymorphisms in several secondary genetic factors associated with CF lung disease severity.
source: Decrease in lung function over time is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality in CF patients (Gilljam et al., 2004; Kerem and Kerem, 1996) and recent genome-wide association studies have identified polymorphisms in several secondary genetic factors associate with CF lung disease severity (Corvol et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corvol et al., 2015 and Sun et al., 2012.

claim: CF patients exhibit gastrointestinal disease manifestations, such as meconium ileus (MI) at birth, and distal intestinal obstructive syndrome (DIOS).
source: CF patients also exhibit gastrointestinal disease manifestations, such as meconium ileus (MI) at birth, and distal intestinal obstructive syndrome (DIOS) (Canale-Zambrano et al., 2007; Werlin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Canale-Zambrano et al., 2007 and Werlin et al., 2010.

claim: The intestinal phenotype of MI can be easily diagnosed in neonates at birth, and is highly heritable (>88%), having minimal environmental influence.
source: The intestinal phenotype of MI can be easily diagnosed in neonates at birth, and is highly heritable (>88%), having minimal environmental influence (Blackman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blackman et al., 2006.

claim: Genome-wide association studies identified SLC6A14, SLC26A9 and SLC9A3 as modifiers of the CF intestinal phenotype.
source: For this reason, it was used in the genome-wide association studies (GWAS), which identified SLC6A14, SLC26A9 and SLC9A3 as modifiers of the CF intestinal phenotype (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: The role for secondary genes in modifying CF disease severity has been studied extensively using CF mouse models.
source: The role for secondary genes in modifying CF disease severity has been studied extensively using CF mouse models (Bradford et al., 2009; Hillesheim et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2015; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Singh et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bradford et al., 2009; Hillesheim et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2015; Rozmahel et al., 1996; Singh et al., 2013; and Walker et al., 2008.

claim: Deletion of the Cftr gene, or knock-in of the mutant F508del Cftr gene, generates significant changes to intestinal pathology.
source: Deletion of the Cftr gene, or knock-in of the mutant F508del Cftr gene, generates significant changes to intestinal pathology (Grubb and Gabriel, 1997; Ratcliff et al., 1993; Scholte et al., 2004; van Doorninck et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grubb and Gabriel, 1997; Ratcliff et al., 1993; Scholte et al., 2004; and van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claim: CF mice have growth retardation when compared to their Wt (wild type) littermates, attributed to malabsorption and decreased secretion of IGF-1.
source: CF mice have growth retardation when compared to their Wt (wild type) littermates, and this has been attributed to malabsorption and decreased secretion of IGF-1 (Canale-Zambrano et al., 2007; Rogan et al., 2010; van Doorninck et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Canale-Zambrano et al., 2007; Rogan et al., 2010; and van Doorninck et al., 1995.

claim: The intestine of CF mice exhibits mucus accumulation, inflammation and goblet cell hyperplasia in the epithelial layers.
source: Histologically, the intestine of CF mice exhibits mucus accumulation, inflammation and goblet cell hyperplasia in the epithelial layers (Grubb and Gabriel, 1997; Ratcliff et al., 1993), and circular smooth muscle hypertrophy in the muscularis externa (Risse et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grubb and Gabriel, 1997 and Ratcliff et al., 1993.

claim: The intestine of CF mice exhibits circular smooth muscle hypertrophy in the muscularis externa.
source: Histologically, the intestine of CF mice exhibits mucus accumulation, inflammation and goblet cell hyperplasia in the epithelial layers (Grubb and Gabriel, 1997; Ratcliff et al., 1993), and circular smooth muscle hypertrophy in the muscularis externa (Risse et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Risse et al., 2012.

claim: The increase in smooth muscle thickness of the intestinal wall is variable in CF mice of different backgrounds, and modifier genes have been attributed to these differences.
source: This increase in smooth muscle thickness of the intestinal wall is variable in CF mice of different backgrounds (Bazett et al., 2015; Risse et al., 2012), and modifier genes have been attributed to these differences.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bazett et al., 2015 and Risse et al., 2012.

claim: Disruption of Slc26a9 caused defects in bicarbonate secretion and fluid absorption in the proximal duodenum, leading to increased mortality in CF mice.
source: Disruption of Slc26a9 caused defects in bicarbonate secretion and fluid absorption in the proximal duodenum, leading to increased mortality in CF mice (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Disruption of Slc9a3 expression improved the CF phenotype of fluid secretion and reversed the intestinal phenotype of CF mice.
source: On the other hand, disruption of Slc9a3 expression improved the CF phenotype of fluid secretion and reversed the intestinal phenotype of CF mice (Bradford et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bradford et al., 2009.

claim: SLC6A14 is a Na+/Cl- dependent neutral and cationic amino acid transporter.
source: SLC6A14 is a Na+/Cl- dependent neutral and cationic amino acid transporter (Karunakaran et al., 2011; Rajan et al., 2000) expressed on the apical membrane of epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Karunakaran et al., 2011 and Rajan et al., 2000.

claim: SLC6A14 is expressed on the apical membrane of epithelial cells.
source: SLC6A14 is a Na+/Cl- dependent neutral and cationic amino acid transporter (Karunakaran et al., 2011; Rajan et al., 2000) expressed on the apical membrane of epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by localization studies in this manuscript.

claim: SLC6A14 is hypothesized to be principally involved in nutrient uptake, due to its broad specificity and concentrative transport mechanisms.
source: It is hypothesized that this amino acid transporter is principally involved in nutrient uptake, due to its broad specificity and concentrative transport mechanisms (Galietta et al., 1998; Rudnick et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Galietta et al., 1998 and Rudnick et al., 2014.

source: Furthermore, it has been studied as a potential drug target in various epithelial cancers, such as colon, breast and pancreats (Babu et al., 2015; Coothankandaswamy et al., 2016; Karunakaran et al., 2011; Karunakaran et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Babu et al., 2015; Coothankandaswamy et al., 2016; Karunakaran et al., 2011; and Karunakaran et al., 2008.

claim: The biological role of SLC6A14 in modifying the CF phenotype has not been interrogated prior to this study.
source: However, to date, the biological role of SLC6A14 in modifying the CF phenotype has not been interrogated.
